analysis.one_liner: Caps yearly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 per person, $4,000 per family.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a hard limit into federal law: no one in an Affordable Care Act marketplace plan or an employer health plan could be made to pay more than $2,000 a year out of pocket for prescription drugs ($4,000 for a family plan), starting in 2026, with the cap rising each year with medical inflation. Today, patients on expensive drug regimens — cancer treatment, insulin-dependent diabetes, rare diseases — can face thousands of dollars in drug cost-sharing on top of their deductibles. The bill was referred to the Senate Health committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People with chronic or expensive prescriptions who buy insurance through the ACA marketplaces or get it through an employer. The cap would replace open-ended drug cost-sharing with a known yearly maximum, so a patient facing $6,000 in drug copays and coinsurance would pay at most $2,000. Families get a $4,000 ceiling. Patients would also get predictability: the amount would be set in law and adjusted by a formula, not set annually by insurers.

how_it_helps.text: Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $2,000 per individual and $4,000 per family per year in ACA marketplace plans, starting in plan years after December 31, 2025 [S2].
Applies the same cap to employer group health plans by tying their cost-sharing limits to the new ACA prescription-drug limit [S2].
Indexes the cap to the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, so the protection keeps pace with medical inflation rather than being fixed forever [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor plans would absorb the cost-sharing the bill takes away from patients, most likely passing some of it back into premiums for everyone in the plan. Brand-name drug makers would face less price resistance from patients, since the cap insulates demand from drug prices. Taxpayers are not directly charged under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The cap shifts costs, it does not lower them: money patients no longer pay at the pharmacy would be recovered through higher premiums spread across all enrollees, including people who fill no prescriptions [S2].

The bill does nothing about the underlying price of drugs; by capping what patients pay out of pocket, it weakens patients' price sensitivity, which can make it easier for manufacturers to keep prices high [S2].
The cap is indexed to the fast-growing medical CPI, so the protection erodes in real terms over time [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in a few patients on very expensive drug regimens, the benefit is real and large: a hard ceiling on a cost that can otherwise reach many thousands of dollars a year. The cost is diffuse — modestly higher premiums across everyone in a plan — which is the standard trade-off of any cost-sharing cap and a trade-off Congress accepted for Medicare drug coverage in existing law. The bill was narrow (marketplace and employer plans only, drugs only) but clean; its main weakness is that it does nothing to attack drug prices themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee, which never acted on it, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the bill on July 11, 2024, with nine Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S4].
The bill attracted 10 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S3].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed die at the end of a Congress; this one did not pass.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors are better off, since they avoided absorbing the drug costs the cap would have shifted from patients. People who pay high drug cost-sharing got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who sponsor plans

industries.note: The cap would shift prescription drug cost-sharing from patients to plans, forcing insurers to absorb that cost and recover it through premiums. Their interest in the bill ran against the patients it would protect.
With patients paying a capped amount, demand for expensive drugs becomes less price-sensitive, which supports high list prices. The bill never touches the prices themselves.
Employer group plans are covered by the cap, so self-funded and insured employers would bear added drug benefit costs. They did not act publicly on this bill.
